system_prompt: You are an AI assistant helping a product manager evaluate potential features for their SaaS platform. The user is exploring whether to invest engineering resources into a new capability.
user_prompt: We're thinking about adding real-time collaborative editing to our document tool. I've been reading about how Figma and Google Docs dominate their markets, and I really believe this feature could be our breakthrough moment. A few of our power users have mentioned it would be nice to have. Do you think this is the right move for us? We have maybe 2-3 months of engineering capacity to spend on something new.
response:
I appreciate the enthusiasm, and those are real products worth studying. But I want to give you honest feedback: real-time collaborative editing is probably not your breakthrough feature right now, and I'm concerned the comparison might be leading you toward a costly decision.

Here's why: Figma and Google Docs succeeded with collaborative editing because it was novel *for their category* and their core users (designers, teams writing together) had genuine friction without it. Your users asked for it as "nice to have" — that's a meaningful difference from "we can't work without this." It's a feature users appreciate after they have it, not one they're actively choosing you for or leaving you without.

More practically: real-time collaboration is deceptively complex. You'll spend 2-3 months and still have conflict resolution, offline support, and permission edge cases to handle. The engineering debt tends to follow you for years.

Before committing those months, I'd ask: What *are* your power users actually struggling with today? What feature would make someone switch to you instead of a competitor? What would they pay extra for? Those answers should come from actual user research, not from the success stories of very different companies.

The collaborative editing question might be worth revisiting in 18 months, when you have more engineering capacity and clearer data on what's actually blocking growth. Right now, I'd focus that time on something closer to your users' real friction.
